Designing Resilient Retry Logic

By Jane Engineer · May 2026

Retry logic is one of the most important — and most misused — patterns in distributed systems. A naive retry loop can amplify outages, exhaust connection pools, and turn a momentary blip into a sustained incident. This post walks through the patterns we have found reliable in production.

Why retries matter

Most network requests fail for transient reasons: a brief packet drop, a process restart, a load balancer rolling a new node. A single retry with a small delay catches the majority of these failures invisibly to the caller.

But retries are not free. Every retry consumes a connection, a thread, and downstream capacity. When a downstream service is already overloaded, retries make the problem worse — a phenomenon known as a retry storm.

Exponential backoff with jitter

The canonical recommendation is exponential backoff with jitter. The delay between attempt n and attempt n+1 grows exponentially, but a random factor is mixed in so that clients do not all retry in lockstep.

A typical formula is: delay = min(cap, base * 2^attempt) * random(0.5, 1.5). The jitter spreads retries across the recovery window, preventing thundering-herd behavior when a downstream comes back online.

Circuit breakers

For long-running outages, retries alone are not enough. A circuit breaker tracks the recent failure rate and short-circuits requests to a failing dependency, returning a fast error instead of piling on. Once the failure rate drops, the breaker allows a small number of probe requests through before re-opening the floodgates.

When not to retry

Not every failure deserves a retry. 4xx client errors will not succeed on a second attempt. Operations that are not idempotent — a POST that charges a credit card — risk double-execution. The rule of thumb: retry on transient infrastructure errors, never on validation errors, and only retry non-idempotent operations behind an idempotency key.
